title: Falling Squares
description: Brute force to optimized: a coordinate-range grid simulation versus direct interval overlap checks against the small number of previously-dropped squares.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Squares are dropped one at a time onto the X-axis, each described by [left, sideLength]. A dropped square falls until it lands on the X-axis or on top of another square, stacking on whichever previously-dropped square (or the ground) is directly beneath any part of it, at the height of the tallest such support. Return, after each square is dropped, the height of the tallest stack so far.

blocks.text: Simulate dropping squares one at a time: each new square's landing height is the tallest height among all previously-dropped squares (or the ground) that it horizontally overlaps, plus its own side length. After each drop, report the tallest stack seen so far.

blocks.title: Analogy: Stacking Boxes of Different Widths on an Uneven Floor
blocks.text: Picture dropping boxes of varying widths onto a floor, one at a time, where each new box lands on top of whichever earlier boxes it overlaps horizontally, resting at the height of the tallest one beneath it, exactly like real stacking with gravity.

blocks.caption: A new square lands on top of the tallest previously-dropped square it overlaps

blocks.text: The first square [1,2] lands on the ground at height 2; the second [2,3] overlaps it and lands at height 2+3=5; the third [6,1] does not overlap either, landing at height 1 (but the tallest overall stays 5). Result: [2, 5, 5].

Before simulating individual unit positions along the x-axis, notice that with only up to 1000 squares (even though coordinates can be huge), checking each new square against every previous one directly is entirely feasible.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A new square's landing height depends only on the tallest PREVIOUSLY DROPPED square it overlaps horizontally, not on every individual unit position beneath it.

Observation 2: Two intervals [l1, r1) and [l2, r2) overlap exactly when l1 is less than r2 AND l2 is less than r1, a simple, direct check.

Observation 3: Checking a new square against every one of the at most 1000 previously-dropped squares directly, taking the maximum height among overlapping ones, gives the correct landing height.

Observation 4: Since squares.length is capped at 1000, this pairwise check costs at most about a million operations total, entirely practical, regardless of how large the coordinate values themselves are.

This leads to checking each new square's overlap directly against every previously-dropped square, computing its landing height from the tallest overlapping one, and tracking the running maximum height.
Simulate the x-axis as a fine grid of individual unit positions, updating the height at every position covered by each dropped square.

items: Maintain a height value for every unit position along the x-axis.
For each dropped square, find the maximum height among the positions it covers, set every covered position to that height plus the side length, and record the new overall maximum.

codes.python:
def falling_squares(positions):
    # Impractical for coordinates up to 10^8; shown to illustrate the brute-force IDEA
    # on a small coordinate range only.
    min_x = min(p[0] for p in positions)
    max_x = max(p[0] + p[1] for p in positions)
    heights = [0] * (max_x - min_x)
    result = []
    overall_max = 0
    for left, side in positions:
        base = max(heights[left - min_x: left - min_x + side], default=0)
        new_height = base + side
        for i in range(left - min_x, left - min_x + side):     # touch every unit position
            heights[i] = new_height
        overall_max = max(overall_max, new_height)
        result.append(overall_max)
    return result

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every unit position covered by a square is updated directly, exactly simulating physical stacking at the finest granularity.
With coordinates up to 10^8, this grid would be far too large to allocate or update in practice.

blocks.text: Limitation: with coordinates up to 10^8, allocating or scanning a grid over the whole range is completely impractical; since only up to 1000 squares exist, working directly with intervals (not individual positions) is both correct and efficient enough.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why grid simulation is unnecessary: a square's landing height only depends on the tallest of the (at most 1000) previously-dropped squares it overlaps, not on individual unit positions.

How to check overlap directly: two intervals [l1, r1) and [l2, r2) overlap exactly when l1 is less than r2 and l2 is less than r1.

The core idea: for each new square, check its overlap directly against every previous square, take the maximum height among overlapping ones as the base, add the new square's side length, and track the running overall maximum.

Maintain a list of previously-dropped squares as (left, right, height) intervals. For each new square, compute its base as the maximum height among all previous squares it horizontally overlaps (0 if none). Its landing height is that base plus its side length. Record it in the list, update the running overall maximum, and append it to the result.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: check overlap directly against every previous square, no grid needed

codes.python:
def falling_squares(positions):
    dropped = []                              # list of (left, right, height)
    result = []
    overall_max = 0
    for left, side in positions:
        right = left + side
        base = 0
        for l, r, h in dropped:                 # check overlap against every previous square directly
            if l < right and left < r:
                base = max(base, h)
        new_height = base + side
        dropped.append((left, right, new_height))
        overall_max = max(overall_max, new_height)
        result.append(overall_max)
    return result

blocks.text: Checking overlap directly with the simple interval condition (one square's left edge before the other's right edge, and vice versa) correctly identifies every previously-dropped square that shares horizontal space with the new one; taking the maximum height among those exactly matches how a physical square would land in reality. Since only up to 1000 squares are ever dropped, this pairwise check remains efficient, entirely independent of how large the coordinate values are.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), checking every pair of squares.
Space: O(n) for the list of dropped squares.

blocks.text: Falling Squares shows that when a coordinate range is huge but the number of actual objects (squares) is small, working directly with intervals and pairwise overlap checks is both correct and efficient, entirely avoiding a coordinate-range-sized data structure.

items: Using a non-strict overlap check (allowing touching edges to count as overlapping), which would incorrectly stack adjacent, non-overlapping squares.
Forgetting to track the running OVERALL maximum height, instead of just each individual square's own landing height.

blocks.text: Explicitly noting that the small bound on the NUMBER of squares (not the coordinate range) is what makes the O(n squared) pairwise approach both correct and efficient is the key constraint to call out.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "coordinates are huge, how do you avoid a grid", think: work with intervals directly, checking overlap pairwise against the small number of actual squares.

Any "large coordinate range, small number of actual objects" problem, solved by working with intervals or coordinate compression rather than a full grid.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(coordinate range times n) time and O(coordinate range) space. The optimized direct interval overlap approach runs in O(n squared) time and O(n) space, both independent of the coordinate range.

items: Pattern: direct interval overlap checks, avoiding a coordinate-range-sized grid.
Core Idea: each new square's landing height is the tallest of every previously-dropped square it horizontally overlaps, plus its own side length, found via direct pairwise interval checks.
Time: O(coordinate range times n) for the brute force, O(n squared) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(coordinate range) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: the small bound on the number of squares, not the coordinate range, is what the solution should scale with.
Interview Difficulty: a good example of choosing the right data representation (intervals, not a grid) based on which quantity is actually small.
One line memory trick: check overlap directly against every previous square; land on the tallest one.
